title: Free college classes for New Yorkers 60 and older
seoTitle: Free College Classes for Seniors in New York
seoDesc: New Yorkers 60+ can audit SUNY classes tuition-free and CUNY classes for about $80 a semester. Campus rules near NJ, OLLI programs and NYC library classes.
dek: At 60, you can sit in on real college classes at SUNY and CUNY campuses for little or nothing. Here are the rules, the fees, and how five campuses near New Jersey handle senior auditors.
keyFacts: SUNY policy: auditors pay no tuition; a $50 registration fee may be charged
Hunter College senior auditors pay $65 plus $15 a semester
Westchester Community College: $52.50 covers up to two audited courses
SUNY Orange senior auditors pay no fees
NYPL Creative Aging workshops for adults 50+ are free
body:
New Yorkers 60 and older can sit in on college classes at SUNY and CUNY campuses for free or close to it. SUNY campuses charge senior auditors no tuition, and CUNY colleges such as Hunter and Queens charge $80 a semester in fees (at Hunter, a $65 general fee plus a $15 consolidated services fee).

Auditing means you attend the class without grades, exams or credit. Seats go to degree students first, so you register late and take what's open. This guide covers what state law and SUNY policy say and how five campuses near New Jersey run their programs. It also covers the CUNY rules, lifelong learning institutes for people 50 and over, and free classes at New York City's three library systems.

What does New York law allow?

Two rules make this possible. State Education Law section 6303 lets community colleges permit people 60 or older to audit courses without tuition, exams, grading or credit, on a space-available basis. Each college president decides how it works on that campus.

For SUNY's state-operated campuses, a SUNY policy on course auditors sets the ground rules. Auditors pay no tuition. A campus may charge a $50 registration fee, plus penalty fees such as late registration or library fines. Students taking the course for credit get priority, and auditors attend without credit and without having to meet course requirements. The policy points to Education Law section 355 for the age 60 rule.

So the deal is similar everywhere, but the details are not. Some campuses waive every fee. Some charge a small one. Many close labs, studios and language classes to auditors.

An audit seat is a front-row view of a real college class, with no tests and no tuition bill.

How does auditing work at SUNY campuses near New Jersey?

Here is what five campuses in Rockland, Westchester, Orange and Ulster counties say on their own pages.

CampusCost to auditWhen you get a seatContact
SUNY Rockland Community CollegeNo tuition; you pay lab and course feesProcessed one week after the semester starts845-574-4328
SUNY Westchester Community College$52.50 a semester, nonrefundable, for up to two coursesNeeds 6 open seats at review; check the page for spring dates914-606-6830
SUNY Orange (Middletown and Newburgh)No feesRegistered after the add/drop period845-341-4140
SUNY PurchaseNo tuition; $50 auditor's fee plus a one-time $30 ID feeWinter 2027 requests by email from December 18 at 1 p.m.registrar@purchase.edu
SUNY New Paltz$50 registration fee waived at 60; technology fee appliesRegistered one week before classes startRecords & Registration

SUNY Rockland

The college waives tuition for adults 60 and older who want to observe credit courses. Auditors still pay lab and other course fees. Seniors fill out the Senior Audit Data Sheet and Registration Form. If a course looks likely to have room, registrations are processed in the order received. Seniors who want credit pay regular tuition. See the Rockland County page for more local help.

SUNY Westchester Community College

The Senior Audit Observer Program is open to people 60 and older, and you show a driver's license as proof of age. Only lecture classes qualify. Classes with a lab, hands-on, noncredit, honors and foreign language classes are out. A class needs six open seats when your application is reviewed, and each class takes no more than two senior auditors. Once approved, pick up a student ID and parking pass at the Security Office on the first floor of the Student Center, 48 hours after you get confirmation. Fall 2026 applications ran August 27 to September 4, so watch the page for spring dates.

SUNY Orange

Orange cites Article 126, section 6303 of state law. Senior auditors pay no fees and are registered after add/drop so degree students get their seats first. Nursing, other health professions courses, private music instruction, P-TECH, honors seminars and lab-heavy courses are excluded. For an online or hybrid class, you need your own computer and reliable internet. The college expects to take spring 2027 forms in late December or early January.

SUNY Purchase and SUNY New Paltz

Purchase lets New York State residents 60 and older take up to two credit-bearing, on-campus courses a semester tuition-free, where space allows. Auditors pay a nonrefundable $50 auditor's fee and a one-time $30 ID processing fee, plus any lab or studio fees and parking. For winter 2027, registration is by email only, starting December 18 at 1 p.m. Forms emailed earlier are not accepted, and all winter courses are online. You get a reply within 24 hours. Auditors can use the library but not the athletic facilities, the campus shuttle or student clubs.

At New Paltz in Ulster County, the $50 audit registration fee is waived for people 60 and older, though the technology fee still applies to all auditors. Studio, lab and performance courses are closed to auditors. Auditors are registered one week before classes start. Your audit form needs signatures from the instructor and the department chair.

How do I sign up to audit a class?

  1. Pick two or three courses. Use the college's public class search. Lecture courses are your surest bet, since labs and studios are often closed to auditors.
  2. Get the senior audit form. Each campus has its own. Some are online, some are a PDF you email or mail.
  3. Gather proof of age. A driver's license works almost everywhere. CUNY colleges also take a birth certificate or passport, and some ask for proof of New York address.
  4. Send it on the right day. Many campuses won't process senior forms until after degree students register. Sending it too early can get it rejected.
  5. Watch your email. At Rockland and Orange, seats are confirmed only after the semester starts or after add/drop. Set up any student account the college sends you so you can see class materials online.
  6. Pay any fee and go to class. Ask the instructor how much they want you to take part. Some welcome discussion and some prefer auditors listen.

How does the CUNY senior audit program work?

Hunter, Queens and the College of Staten Island each let people 60 and older audit undergraduate courses tuition-free, on a space-available basis. You pay small fees each semester instead. Other CUNY colleges run similar programs, so ask the admissions office at the campus nearest you.

  • Hunter College, Manhattan. Open to New York State residents 60 and older. You pay a $65 general fee and a $15 consolidated services fee each semester, plus your own books. Apply online with proof of age, proof of New York address and proof of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) shots. Priority deadlines are August 10 for fall, January 15 for spring and July 5 for summer. There's no winter session for senior learners. Registration opens on the second day of each semester.
  • Queens College. Open to New York State residents 60 and older who finished high school. The cost is $80 a semester, billed at registration, and you can audit up to 9 credits with department approval. The spring deadline is Thursday, January 21. First-time auditors born in or after 1957 need immunization records, and everyone submits a meningitis form once. Graduate courses are not open to auditors. Call Admissions at 718-997-5600.
  • College of Staten Island. Open to people 60 and older as of the first day of the semester who meet the city or state residency rules. The nonrefundable administrative fee is $65 a semester, plus the consolidated service fee. A Medicare card, driver's license or birth certificate proves age.

At these colleges, seniors who want credit pay regular tuition. At the College of Staten Island, you can't be an auditor and a credit student in the same semester. Graduate courses are charged at the graduate rate.

CUNY collegeFees per semesterNotes
Hunter College$65 plus $15NYS residents 60+; MMR proof required
Queens College$80Up to 9 credits; high school diploma required
College of Staten Island$65 plus consolidated service feeUndergraduate courses only, audit basis

What lifelong learning programs are there for people 50 and over?

If your parent wants classmates their own age, lifelong learning institutes at public colleges are a good fit. They run noncredit workshops and lectures, often led by members.

  • Osher Lifelong Learning Institute (OLLI) at Stony Brook University, Suffolk County. For adults 50 and older. Membership is $375 for the year, $200 for a fall or spring term, or $100 for summer. Members choose up to six in-person workshops and unlimited Zoom workshops a semester, plus faculty lectures and day trips. Call 631-632-6554.
  • Mainstream at SUNY Westchester Community College. Noncredit courses designed for adults over 50, in enrichment, personal growth, history and culture, and sports and fitness. Call 914-606-6830.
  • Collegium for Lifelong Learning, Valhalla. A membership group created in 2004 by college volunteers who wanted to mix serious study with social time. It meets at the Knollwood Center on the Valhalla campus. Call 914-606-6748.

What classes do New York City libraries offer older adults?

All three library systems run Creative Aging classes for older adults. NYPL says its workshops are free. Brooklyn uses an age cutoff of 55 and NYPL uses 50.

  • New York Public Library (Bronx, Manhattan, Staten Island). Creative Aging workshops for adults 50 and older run 5 to 8 weeks, and NYPL recommends going to every session. This fall's classes include clay at Allerton Library in the Bronx, a writing workshop called Writing to Remember at Riverdale and the 58th Street Library, and watercolor at South Beach Library on Staten Island. Register online or call the branch to ask about drop-in space.
  • Brooklyn Public Library. Services for Older Adults plans programs for patrons over 55, in person and online. That includes multi-session Creative Aging art workshops led by a professional teaching artist and Technology For All help with phones, email and Zoom. Call 718-938-2525 for tech help, in English or Spanish.
  • Queens Public Library. Grant-funded Creative Aging courses include drawing, watercolor, collage, quilting, sewing, acrylic painting and memoir writing. Call Older Adult Services at 718-464-0084 or 718-776-6800.

If getting to the branch is the hard part, Brooklyn Public Library runs Books by Mail for people who are homebound or have a visual disability. Outside the city, ask your local library and your county Office for the Aging. Our senior centers guide covers the free classes many centers run as well.

What should you know before the first class?

  • Expect to wait. Seats are confirmed after degree students register, often in the first week of classes.
  • Have a backup course. Popular classes fill. Westchester needs six open seats before it will add a senior auditor.
  • Budget for small costs. Books, lab fees at Rockland, the fees at Purchase and the technology fee at New Paltz are not waived.
  • Don't drop or add on your own. Queens College asks auditors to email auditors@qc.cuny.edu instead of changing classes in CUNYfirst.
  • Know the refund rules. Queens says auditors get no refund once classes start. Westchester's $52.50 is nonrefundable.
  • Don't show up before you're registered. Purchase asks auditors not to attend a class before they are officially registered.

For a parent who stopped driving, check the bus route before signing up. Riders 65 and older pay half fare on MTA buses and subways with a Reduced-Fare OMNY card, as our MTA reduced fare guide explains, and our guide for older drivers covers other ways to get around.

faq.q: Can my mom take free classes at SUNY Rockland Community College?
faq.a: Yes, if she is 60 or older. Rockland Community College waives tuition for seniors who audit credit courses, though she pays any lab or course fees. Registrations are processed one week after the semester starts. Call Records and Registration at 845-574-4328.

faq.q: How does my dad audit a class at Hunter College in Manhattan?
faq.a: He must be a New York State resident aged 60 or older. He applies online with proof of age, proof of address and proof of MMR shots, then registers on the second day of the semester. Fees are $65 plus $15 a semester. The spring priority deadline is January 15.

faq.q: Is college free for seniors in New York?
faq.a: Auditing is free or nearly free. SUNY campuses charge senior auditors no tuition, and some charge small fees. Hunter and Queens charge $80 a semester in fees, and the College of Staten Island charges $65 plus its consolidated service fee. Taking a course for credit costs regular tuition.

faq.q: Do senior auditors get grades or credit?
faq.a: No. Auditors attend without exams, grades or credit. Some instructors invite auditors to join discussions and some prefer that they listen, so ask on the first day.

faq.q: Can I audit online classes at SUNY?
faq.a: Often, yes. SUNY Orange allows online and hybrid courses if you have your own computer and internet. SUNY Purchase's winter 2027 courses are all online, with email registration opening December 18 at 1 p.m.

faq.q: Are there art and writing classes for older adults at the Queens library?
faq.a: Yes. Queens Public Library offers grant-funded Creative Aging courses such as drawing, watercolor, quilting and memoir writing. Ask the library about any cost. Call Older Adult Services at 718-464-0084 or 718-776-6800 to find one near you.

title: Working after 60 in New York: job help, pay limits and your rights
seoTitle: Jobs After 60 in New York: Help, Limits and Rights
seoDesc: Job help for New Yorkers 55+: SCSEP paid training, NYC Aging programs, Career Centers, 2027 Social Security earnings limits and age discrimination rules.
dek: New York has paid job training for low-income workers 55 and older, free Career Centers for everyone, and strong age discrimination laws. Here is how they work, and how a paycheck affects Social Security.
keyFacts: SCSEP: age 55+, family income up to 125% of poverty, about 20 paid hours a week
2027 Social Security earnings limit under full retirement age: $25,560
In the year you reach full retirement age in 2027: $67,920
NY Human Rights Law covers every employer, regardless of size
NY unemployment insurance maximum: $869 a week, up to 26 weeks
body:
You can keep working after 60 in New York, and there is free public help to find the job. Job seekers 55 and older with low income can get paid, part-time training through the Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP), and anyone can walk into a New York State Department of Labor Career Center.

Before taking a job, check how the paycheck affects Social Security. If you claimed benefits before full retirement age, earning over $25,560 in 2027 means some benefits are held back for a while. This guide covers the job programs, the earnings limits, your rights against age discrimination, and what unemployment pays if a job ends.

What is SCSEP, and who qualifies?

SCSEP is a federal work-based training program for older workers, authorized under Title V of the Older Americans Act. In New York it runs through the New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA), local partners and national nonprofit grantees.

To qualify, the U.S. Department of Labor says you must be:

  • At least 55
  • Unemployed
  • Living on a family income of no more than 125% of the federal poverty level

Participants work an average of 20 hours a week at nonprofit and public sites. The Department of Labor names schools, hospitals, day-care centers and senior centers as examples. Pay is the highest of the federal, state or local minimum wage. NYSOFA says participants get an Individual Employment Plan, training for the assignment, supportive services, annual physicals and help moving into a regular job. Participation is limited to 48 months unless an extension is authorized.

Enrollment priority goes first to veterans and some spouses of veterans. After that it goes to people who are 65 or older, have a disability, have limited English or low literacy, live in a rural area, are homeless or at risk, have poor job prospects, could not find work through job centers, or left prison or jail within the past five years.

Where do I apply outside New York City?

NYSOFA posts a list of SCSEP providers by region. You can also use the Older Worker Program Finder on CareerOneStop or call the federal help line at 1-877-872-5627. Near New Jersey, Westchester County's SCSEP page says to call a peer counselor at the Urban League of Westchester, 914-428-5850. NYSOFA's regional contact list names MaturityWorks, run by the nonprofit The WorkPlace, for the state-funded program in Rockland and Westchester, at 203-610-8588. Elsewhere, your county Office for the Aging or the New York State Office for the Aging at 1-800-342-9871 can point you to the local provider.

SCSEP pays you while you train. The assignment is meant as a bridge to a regular, unsubsidized job.

What does NYC Aging offer job seekers?

NYC Aging runs several Older Adult Workforce Programs for the five boroughs. For any of them, call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and ask for employment services.

  • Older Adult Employment Program. This is the city's SCSEP program, for New York City residents 55 and older who are unemployed and meet the 125% poverty income limit. It offers classes in digital and financial skills, customer service, resumes and interviews, plus an internship at a nonprofit or City agency. In-person information sessions are held the second Thursday of every month at 10 a.m. Questions go to jobs@aging.nyc.gov.
  • Silver Corps. An AmeriCorps program for city residents 55 and older who are unemployed or underemployed. You volunteer at least 10 hours a week at a nonprofit or government agency and get job-readiness training, credentialing and job coaching.
  • Silver Stars. Part-time, temporary work at City agencies for fully retired City employees who receive a City pension. You keep collecting your pension. Search "silver" on the NYC Careers job site.
  • Civic Engagement Employment Service (ReServe). For city residents 50 and older who are unemployed. Assignments at nonprofits and City agencies usually run 10 to 20 hours a week and pay minimum wage.

How can a Department of Labor Career Center help?

Career Centers offer free help with the job search across the state. The Department of Labor's Career Center locator lists 90 of them, which you can filter by region or county, and many offer virtual services too.

NYSOFA says it and the Department of Labor have combined forces in a new Older Adult Worker unit to support older New Yorkers who want to work. The Department of Labor's page for older adult workers has a resume guide and interviewing tips for older workers, plus sections on training, ageism at work and working while retired. For more help, it points you to your local Career Center.

  1. Decide on hours and income. Before you apply, figure out how many hours you want and how pay will affect Social Security, SNAP or other benefits.
  2. Check SCSEP first if money is tight. If you're 55 or older, unemployed and low income, call the local SCSEP provider or, in the city, Aging Connect.
  3. Book a Career Center visit. Use the Department of Labor's Career Center locator. Bring your work history and an updated resume, or ask for help writing one.
  4. Ask about virtual help. The Career Center locator shows which centers offer virtual services you can use from home.
  5. Look at programs for your old employer. Retired New York City workers can look at Silver Stars.
  6. Keep records. Save job postings, dates and names. If you suspect age bias, the Division of Human Rights will ask for dates and names.

How does a paycheck affect Social Security before full retirement age?

If you're under full retirement age and earn more than a yearly limit, Social Security holds back part of your benefit. Once you reach full retirement age, there is no limit at all.

Situation2026 limit2027 limitWhat Social Security withholds
Under full retirement age all year$24,480$25,560$1 for every $2 over the limit
Year you reach full retirement age (months before your birthday month)$65,160$67,920$1 for every $3 over the limit
From the month you reach full retirement ageNo limitNo limitNothing

Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For people born in 1959, it's 66 and 10 months.

Only wages and net self-employment earnings count, including bonuses, commissions and vacation pay. Social Security does not count pensions, annuities, investment income, interest, veterans benefits or other government or military retirement benefits.

The money held back isn't lost. When you reach full retirement age, Social Security raises your monthly benefit to credit the months it withheld. And if a later year of work is one of your highest-earning years, it recalculates your benefit and pays any increase.

What does that look like in real numbers?

Say your mom is 63 all of 2027, gets Social Security and earns $31,560 at a part-time job. That's $6,000 over the $25,560 limit. Social Security would withhold $3,000 of her benefits for the year, $1 for every $2 over. If she waits to work more hours until the year she turns 67, a much higher limit applies. Social Security has an earnings test calculator to try her own numbers, and our Social Security 2027 guide covers this year's other changes.

Medicare has its own sign-up rules at 65, separate from when you claim Social Security. You can delay Part B if you are covered by an employer group health plan. Our Medicare costs guide has the 2027 premiums.

What protects older workers from age discrimination?

New York's Human Rights Law bans age discrimination in employment, and it covers every employer in the state regardless of size, including state and local government. Federal law adds protection for workers 40 and older at employers with 20 or more employees.

Under the federal Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the ban covers hiring, firing, pay, job assignments, promotions, layoffs, training and benefits. Harassment over age is illegal when it is so frequent or severe that it creates a hostile or offensive workplace. A policy that applies to everyone can also be illegal if it hurts workers 40 and older and isn't based on a reasonable factor other than age.

  • New York State Division of Human Rights. Filing is free and you don't need a lawyer. For acts on or after February 15, 2024, you have three years from the most recent incident to report. The Call Center at 844-697-3471 can take your report by phone, or you can use the online form.
  • U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC). The usual deadline to file a charge is 180 days, which may be extended by state laws.

Before you report, the Division asks you to gather the dates, the legal name and contact details of the employer or people involved, and a clear explanation of why you believe age was the reason. Its examples include an unfair comment from a boss, or evidence that other people were treated better in the same situation.

What does unemployment pay if a job ends?

New York unemployment insurance pays up to $869 a week, depending on your past earnings. Benefits last up to 26 weeks within a 12-month period from when you first file.

  • How to file. Apply online through the Department of Labor. For general questions, the Telephone Claims Center is at 1-888-209-8124. On Fridays the center focuses on processing claims.
  • What you need. Your Social Security number, a driver's license or other government ID, and your work history for the last 18 months, with employer names, addresses, dates and pay.
  • The first week. It's an unpaid waiting week. You still certify for it and complete three work search activities.
  • Every week after. Certify your claim each week, keep up your required work search activities and go to your mandatory appointment with a Department of Labor Career Advisor.
  • Pensions. Tell the Department of Labor if you receive or apply for a pension or workers' compensation, because either may change your benefit.
  • Taxes. You can choose optional tax withholding when you set up payment.

If your parent is on a fixed income and a job falls through, the SNAP guide and the HEAP heating help guide cover other support worth checking.

faq.q: How can my mom in the Bronx find a part-time job at 62?
faq.a: Call NYC Aging's Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and ask for employment services. If she is unemployed and low income, the Older Adult Employment Program offers paid training and an internship. ReServe places city residents 50 and older in part-time roles of 10 to 20 hours a week. The Department of Labor's Career Center locator also lists free centers in the Bronx and across the city.

faq.q: Can my dad in Westchester get paid job training at 58?
faq.a: Yes, if he is unemployed and his family income is no more than 125% of the federal poverty level. The Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP) pays the highest of the federal, state or local minimum wage for an average of 20 hours a week. Westchester County's SCSEP page says to call a peer counselor at the Urban League of Westchester, 914-428-5850.

faq.q: How much can I earn on Social Security in 2027?
faq.a: If you are under full retirement age all year, the 2027 limit is $25,560, and Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 above it. In the year you reach full retirement age, the limit is $67,920 for the months before your birthday month, with $1 withheld for every $3 above it. After that there is no limit.

faq.q: Can an employer in New York refuse to hire me because of my age?
faq.a: No. The New York State Human Rights Law bans age discrimination in hiring and on the job, and it covers every employer in the state regardless of size. Report it to the Division of Human Rights at 844-697-3471 within three years. Filing is free.

faq.q: Will my pension reduce my unemployment benefits in New York?
faq.a: It can. The Department of Labor says pension payments may affect your benefit amount, and you must tell it if you receive or apply for a pension. Report it when you file, and the Department will figure the effect on your claim.

faq.q: What is the Silver Stars program?
faq.a: Silver Stars, run by NYC Aging, offers part-time, temporary work at City agencies to fully retired New York City employees who receive a City pension. Participants keep collecting their pension. Search "silver" on the NYC Careers job site, or email silverstars@aging.nyc.gov.

title: Older drivers in New York: renewal, vision tests and the keys talk
seoTitle: Older Drivers in NY: License Renewal and Safety Rules
seoDesc: New York has no age-based road test. How license renewal and the vision test work, how families can ask the DMV for a review, and the 10% insurance course.
dek: New York never ends a license because of age. Here is how renewal and the vision test work, how a family member can ask the DMV to review a driver, and how to plan for life after driving.
keyFacts: No age-based road test; DMV acts only on driving ability
Licenses last 8 years; renew 1 year early to 2 years late
Vision test at every renewal: at least 20/40, glasses allowed
Families use form DS-7, mailed to the DMV Medical Review Unit
Defensive driving course: 10% off base insurance rate for 3 years
body:
New York does not take away a driver's license because of age, and there is no automatic road test at any birthday. Every driver renews every eight years and must pass a vision test, with at least 20/40 vision in one or both eyes, with or without glasses.

If a family member or doctor is worried, they can ask the DMV in writing to re-evaluate the driver, and the DMV will decide based on driving ability. This guide covers renewal and the vision rule, how a review request works, the defensive driving insurance discount, warning signs, and other ways to get around once the keys are put away.

Does New York require older drivers to retest?

No. The DMV says it will not remove driving privileges based on age, or on any standard except driving ability. There is no age at which a road test or written test is required just for renewal.

What New York does require of every driver at renewal is a vision test. The DMV can also require a re-evaluation of any driver, of any age, when it has "reasonable grounds" to believe the person is not qualified to drive. Under the DMV's rules, that means a specific reason tied to driving, such as an incident or behavior reported by a doctor, a police officer or someone who knows or has observed the driver.

The DMV also runs a crash re-examination program for drivers of all ages who have three or more reportable crashes within 18 months. Those drivers are called in for an interview and possible eye, written and road tests.

In New York, age alone never ends a license. Ability does.

How do you renew a license in New York?

A New York driver license is valid for eight years. You can renew online, by mail or at a DMV office, from one year before it expires to two years after.

RuleWhat the DMV says
How long a license lasts8 years
Renewal windowUp to 1 year before and 2 years after expiration
Vision standardAt least 20/40 in either or both eyes, with or without corrective lenses
Vision result good for12 months (an eye doctor may set 6 months)
Class D renewal fee$64.50, or $80.50 in the MCTD counties (the five boroughs, Dutchess, Nassau, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Suffolk and Westchester)
Expired 2 years or moreMust apply as a new driver, with written test, pre-licensing course and road test

How does the vision test work?

Your parent can take the vision test at a DMV office, or have it done by a provider. Providers enrolled in the DMV Online Vision Registry send results electronically, so the renewal can be done online without entering test details. Your parent can also have a physician, physician assistant, ophthalmologist, optometrist, optician, registered nurse or nurse professional fill out a Vision Test Report (MV-619). Find enrolled providers with the DMV's Vision Registry Locator by ZIP code.

If glasses are needed to pass, a "B" (corrective lenses) restriction goes on the license. If an eye care professional reports that night vision is impaired, the DMV adds a "Daylight driving only" restriction.

  1. Check the date. Look at the expiration date on the license and watch for the DMV renewal notice in the mail.
  2. Get the vision test. Use a Vision Registry provider, or have a qualified professional complete form MV-619. Results are good for 12 months.
  3. Pick how to renew. Renew online through the DMV or MyDMV, or mail the renewal notice, vision report and a check payable to "Commissioner of Motor Vehicles" to NYS DMV, 207 Genesee Street, Suite 6, Utica, NY 13501-2874.
  4. Go in person if needed. An office visit is required to switch to a REAL ID or Enhanced license, update the photo or change license class.
  5. Print the temporary license. After renewing online, you can print a temporary license that is valid for 60 days.

Driving on an expired license is costly. The DMV lists fines of $25 to $40 if it has been 60 days or less, and $75 to $300 after that, plus surcharges.

How can a family member report an unsafe driver to the DMV?

A family member, neighbor or friend uses form DS-7, Request for Driver Review, and mails the signed original to the DMV's Medical Review Unit. The DMV does not accept these requests by phone or email.

The form asks for the driver's name, address and date of birth, your name, address, phone and relationship, and specific incidents with dates and places. You can list other people who agree. The DMV will not act unless all four parts are complete, and it must include your name and signature. The form warns that the review may lead to suspension or revocation.

Mail it to: Medical Review Unit, NYS DMV, 6 Empire State Plaza, Room 337, Albany, NY 12228.

What happens after a report?

  • A DMV license examiner where the driver lives reviews the form. If there is a valid reason, the driver gets a certified letter to come in for an interview.
  • A vision test is required. The letter may also ask the driver to bring a Physician's Statement (MV-80), a registered and inspected car, and a licensed driver.
  • At the interview, the examiner explains what was reported and lets the driver respond. The examiner can require a written test and a road test.
  • If the driver doesn't show up, the license is suspended until they appear. If they fail the vision or written test, it is suspended until they pass.
  • If the driver fails the road test, the license is revoked. The driver can reapply after at least 30 days.

The DMV says that when a report comes from someone other than a physician, it considers each case separately and does not act without first re-evaluating the driver.

Can a doctor report a driver?

Yes. Doctors use form DS-6, and police use form DS-5. The DMV notes that New York law does not require doctors to report impaired drivers. If a physician reports a condition that affects driving, the DMV can suspend the license until a physician certifies the condition is treated or controlled.

What is the defensive driving insurance discount?

New York's Point and Insurance Reduction Program (PIRP), also called the defensive driving course, cuts the base rate of auto insurance premiums by 10% each year for three years. It can also reduce up to 4 points when calculating a suspension.

Courses are offered by private companies and organizations approved by the DMV, in a classroom, online or by other methods. The classroom version runs 320 minutes, and there is no test. Fees vary by provider. A few rules from the DMV:

  • Take it once every 36 months to keep the insurance discount.
  • Only the principal operator on a policy gets the 10% reduction.
  • Give the certificate to the insurer within 90 days so the discount starts from the course date.
  • Points don't come off the record. Four are subtracted only for figuring a suspension.

The DMV also points older drivers to courses such as the AARP Driver Safety Program, AAA's Safe Driving for Mature Operators and the National Safety Council's Coaching the Mature Driver. It suggests asking your insurer whether it offers a discount for older driver classes.

What are the warning signs it may be time to stop?

The DMV lists signs that driving skills are slipping. It says to be concerned if a driver:

  • has a number of minor crashes or near misses
  • can't concentrate, or has wandering thoughts
  • can't easily read standard road signs
  • gets lost or confused on familiar roads
  • notices other drivers often honking
  • hears concern from family, friends or police

There may be a middle step. The DMV suggests driving in daylight only, avoiding rush hour, sticking to familiar roads, taking shorter trips and using roads with lower speed limits. It also recommends a behind-the-wheel evaluation by a driver rehabilitation specialist, often an occupational therapist at a hospital or clinic. Health insurance normally pays for that evaluation if the person has a medical diagnosis and a doctor's referral, so check the plan. The therapist doesn't report results to the DMV without the driver's written consent.

Ask about medicines and eyes first

The DMV notes that many medicines, even over the counter, can impair driving, and that cataracts and other vision problems can quickly affect it. New glasses or a medicine change sometimes solve the problem. Ask the doctor or pharmacist for a review.

How do you talk with a parent about giving up the keys?

Start early, keep it about safety and independence, and come with a plan for getting around. The DMV says a license is often a symbol of independence, and that stopping after many years is a big adjustment.

  • Pick a calm moment. Not right after a scare, and not in front of others.
  • Use specifics. Name what you saw, like a missed stop sign on a familiar road.
  • Bring in the doctor. A doctor or a driving evaluation can give a neutral opinion.
  • Have rides lined up. Map out how your parent will get to the grocery store, doctor, place of worship and friends.
  • Swap the license for an ID. The DMV lets drivers exchange a license, current or expired within two years, for a non-driver photo ID that serves the same identification purpose. Apply by mail or at a DMV office.

What are the other ways to get around?

  • Reduced fare transit. Riders 65 and older pay half fare on MTA subways and buses. See our MTA reduced fare guide, which also covers some upstate systems.
  • Paratransit. In NYC, people whose disability keeps them off buses and subways may qualify for Access-A-Ride shared rides. See our Access-A-Ride guide.
  • County senior rides. Many county Offices for the Aging offer or point to senior rides. In Suffolk, for example, the towns run senior transportation, with medical appointments given priority. Find the number on your county page, such as Rockland, Westchester or Orange.
  • Senior center rides. Some senior centers provide transportation. See our senior centers guide.

If you aren't sure where to start, NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 can point you to local transportation, and our caregiver support guide covers help for families.

faq.q: How do I report my dad's unsafe driving to the DMV in Westchester?
faq.a: Fill out DMV form DS-7, Request for Driver Review, with specific incidents, dates and places, sign it, and mail the original to Medical Review Unit, NYS DMV, 6 Empire State Plaza, Room 337, Albany, NY 12228. The DMV does not take reports by phone or email, and your name and signature are required.

faq.q: Does my mom in Staten Island need a road test to renew her license?
faq.a: No. New York has no age-based road test. She needs to pass a vision test, with at least 20/40 in one or both eyes, with or without glasses. She can test at a DMV office or with a Vision Registry provider, then renew online, by mail or in person.

faq.q: At what age do you have to stop driving in New York?
faq.a: There is no set age. The DMV says it will not remove driving privileges based on age or any standard except driving ability. A driver can be re-evaluated when the DMV gets a specific report from a doctor, police officer or someone who knows the driver.

faq.q: How much is the defensive driving discount in New York?
faq.a: Completing a DMV-approved Point and Insurance Reduction Program course reduces the base rate of auto insurance premiums by 10% each year for three years. Take it once every 36 months to keep the discount. Only the principal operator on a policy gets the reduction.

faq.q: Will the DMV tell my parent who reported them?
faq.a: The DS-7 form requires your name, signature and relationship to the driver, and the DMV may contact you. At the interview, the examiner explains the information that was received and lets the driver respond. Ask the DMV about confidentiality before you file.

faq.q: What can my parent use as ID after giving up driving?
faq.a: A New York State non-driver photo ID. The DMV lets drivers exchange a current license, or one that expired within the last two years, for a non-driver ID by mail or at a DMV office. It provides the same proof of identification as a driver license.

title: Senior centers in New York: meals, classes and how to find one
seoTitle: Senior Centers in New York: Meals, Classes, How to Join
seoDesc: New York senior centers are open to anyone 60+. Free NYC older adult centers, county meal sites, suggested contributions and how to find one near you.
dek: Anyone 60 or older in New York can join a senior center for lunch, classes and company, with no income test. Here is what centers offer, what meals cost and how to find one in your county or borough.
keyFacts: Community dining is open to anyone 60+, with no income test
Meals are free; a voluntary contribution is suggested
NYC has more than 300 older adult centers and affiliated sites
Meals are served at about 1,000 locations across New York State
NY Connects: 1-800-342-9871; NYC Aging Connect: 212-244-6469
body:
Senior centers in New York are open to anyone 60 or older, and you do not need to show your income to join. They serve a hot lunch on weekdays, run classes and exercise programs, and have staff who help members sign up for benefits.

In New York City they are called older adult centers (OACs), funded by NYC Aging, and membership is free. Everywhere else, your county Office for the Aging runs or funds senior centers and community dining sites, where lunch costs nothing but you are invited to give a small, voluntary contribution. This guide covers what centers offer, what the meals cost, and how to find one in your county or borough.

What does a senior center in New York offer?

Most centers offer a nutritious midday meal, social activities, classes, fitness programs and help with benefits. The exact mix depends on the center, so call the one near you for its schedule.

NYC Aging says its more than 300 older adult centers and affiliated sites across the five boroughs provide healthy meals, activities, classes, fitness programs and social services. The classes and activities it lists include:

  • Arts and crafts, music and theater arts
  • Computer classes
  • Dominos, bingo, chess and ping-pong
  • Gardening
  • Recreational day trips
  • Holiday and birthday celebrations

For health, NYC Aging lists walking clubs, yoga, chair exercises, tai chi, dance and Zumba, plus chronic disease self-management classes for people with arthritis, diabetes and high blood pressure, and falls prevention workshops. Staff also help members with benefits such as Medicare and Medicaid, the rent freeze program (SCRIE) and SNAP. On-site and virtual mental health services are offered at over 80 centers through NYC Aging's Mental Health Initiative.

Outside the city, county programs look similar. Westchester County says many of its congregate dining centers add social and educational activities such as exercise programs, dance, arts and crafts, health promotion and outings. Suffolk County describes its congregate programs as a nutritious midday meal plus a chance for socialization and recreation, often with seminars too.

You do not need to be lonely, low-income or frail to walk in. If you are 60, the door is open.

Who can go, and what does lunch cost?

Anyone 60 or older can eat at a community dining site in New York, and it is not an income-based program. The New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) says there is no charge for the meals, but each person is offered the chance to make a suggested voluntary contribution.

A few family members can come too. According to NYSOFA:

  • A spouse can get meals even if he or she is under 60.
  • A person with a disability younger than 60 who lives with an older adult may use the dining site.
  • At a dining site inside housing mainly for older adults, residents with disabilities may also get meals.

State rules protect people who can't pay. NYSOFA's contribution policy says no service can be denied or affected by a person's inability or unwillingness to contribute, contributions are kept confidential, and a locked box must be available at group meal sites. Reminder letters or calls asking for money are not allowed, and you can't be required to show your income.

WhereWhat the official page says about cost
New York City older adult centersMembership is free for New Yorkers 60 and older
Erie County (Stay Fit Dining)$3.50 contribution suggested, not required; advance reservations required
St. Lawrence County$3 suggested voluntary contribution for people 60 and older; $5 guest fee for anyone under 60; 24-hour reservation requested
Westchester CountySmall suggested contribution, voluntary; pre-registration required
Suffolk CountyNo fee; participants are encouraged to make a voluntary contribution

How do I find an older adult center in New York City?

Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NY) or 311, or search the NYC Aging online service finder by address. Both can point you to the center closest to home.

Centers are run by local community organizations, and NYC Aging says centers in diverse neighborhoods serve culturally aligned meals that reflect the community. All meals are reviewed by NYC Aging nutrition staff. Some centers also serve breakfast or dinner, or offer grab-and-go meals.

NYC Aging also funds centers for specific groups, including SAGE centers and the Queens Center for Gay Seniors for LGBTQ+ older adults, and VISIONS at Selis Manor Senior Center for older adults who are blind or have low vision.

What is a NORC?

A naturally occurring retirement community (NORC) is a housing development or building that, over time, has become home to many older adults. NYC Aging says there are around 60 NORCs in the city with a social service provider on site, and it funds 36 of them. Funded NORCs offer case management, help with benefits, health care management and health promotion such as blood pressure screenings, yoga and tai chi. If your parent's building is a NORC, the services may be right downstairs.

Borough pages on this site list the local numbers: Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island.

How do I find a senior center outside New York City?

Call your county Office for the Aging, or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, which connects you to the local office. NYSOFA says meals are served up to five days a week at about 1,000 locations statewide, in senior centers, senior clubs, senior housing complexes, town halls and other community spots.

Some counties post their sites online. A few examples from county pages:

  • Rockland County. The Office for the Aging lists congregate meal providers, including Meals on Wheels Programs and Services of Rockland in Nanuet (845-624-6325) and the Martin Luther King Multi Purpose Center in Spring Valley (845-425-8910). Its registered dietitian, reachable at 845-364-2115, offers nutrition counseling at meal sites, at home or by phone. See the Rockland County page.
  • Westchester County. The Department of Senior Programs and Services posts a site directory, from the Fox Senior Center in Mount Kisco to the Peter Chema Senior Nutrition Center in Yonkers. Meals are served five or more days a week. See the Westchester County page.
  • Suffolk County. More than 30 nutrition programs. Call 631-853-8227 to find one. The county says many of its nutrition programs provide transportation. See the Suffolk County page.
  • Erie County. Stay Fit Dining serves weekday noon meals at senior centers across the county. To register, call the site nearest you. For food worries, call NY Connects at 716-858-8526. See the Erie County page.

Many towns also run their own senior centers and clubs. Our town pages list senior centers town by town, and every county page lists the Office for the Aging number.

  1. Find the office. Open your parent's county page on this site, or call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. In the five boroughs, call 212-244-6469 or 311.
  2. Ask for the closest sites. Ask which senior centers or dining sites are nearest, which days they serve lunch, and whether any offer rides.
  3. Reserve the meal. Many counties require a reservation, sometimes a day ahead. Erie, Westchester and St. Lawrence all say so.
  4. Ask for the calendar. Request the monthly activity schedule and menu so you can pick a good first day, like a class or celebration.
  5. Go together the first time. A first visit is easier with company. Introduce your parent to the site manager and ask about special diets.
  6. Ask about other help. Staff can often help with SNAP, Medicare, Medicaid and more. Bring questions.

Can a senior center help if my parent can't get there?

Yes, in two ways. Some centers provide rides, and people who can't shop or cook may qualify for home-delivered meals.

NYSOFA says some community sites provide transportation for people who need help getting to a meal location. In New York City, NYC Aging says some centers offer transportation to essential medical and social service appointments. Reduced-fare transit can also help; see our MTA reduced fare guide and Access-A-Ride guide.

NYSOFA says home-delivered meals are for older New Yorkers who can't prepare meals for themselves, for example after a hospital stay. Unlike lunch at a center, they require an interview with the local office to see if your parent qualifies. That same interview can turn up other services, such as in-home help through EISEP. Start with NY Connects.

Food help beyond lunch

NYSOFA's Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program gives eligible low-income adults 60 and older $25 in coupons once a year for fresh produce at participating farmers' markets. Booklets come out in July, can be used through November and go first come, first served. Ask the Office for the Aging or the center. For grocery money, see our SNAP guide.

What should families know before the first visit?

Expect a mix of regulars and newcomers, and a set lunch time. Call ahead, because schedules, menus and services differ from center to center.

  • Lunch is usually around midday. Erie County serves at noon. St. Lawrence County sites list 11:30 a.m. Arrive a little early.
  • Special diets. In Westchester, for example, menus are planned by a registered dietitian nutritionist. Ask what the center can do for diabetic, low-sodium or kosher needs before you go.
  • Nutrition counseling. NYSOFA says registered dietitians offer private counseling on diabetes, weight and healthy eating, and you don't have to eat the meals to meet with one.
  • Volunteering counts. Some older adults start by helping at the meal site or driving meals. NYSOFA says local programs rely on volunteers.
  • A slow start is fine. If your dad doesn't like the first visit, try a different day or another center. Activities change week to week.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Assuming it costs money. Contributions are voluntary. No one should be turned away for not paying.
  • Showing up without a reservation. Many counties need a day's notice to plan meals.
  • Calling the wrong office. In the five boroughs it is NYC Aging. Elsewhere it is the county Office for the Aging.
  • Stopping at lunch. Center staff often know about local rides, legal help, caregiver programs and benefits. Ask.

If you care for a parent and need a break, our caregiver support guide covers respite and support groups, and our free and discounted guide lists other ways to save.

faq.q: How do I find a senior center for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 or 311, or use the NYC Aging service finder online and enter her address. Older adult center membership is free for New Yorkers 60 and older. Ask the center for its monthly calendar and whether it serves breakfast, dinner or grab-and-go meals.

faq.q: Is there a senior lunch program near my dad in Rockland County?
faq.a: Yes. The Rockland County Office for the Aging lists congregate meal providers including Meals on Wheels Programs and Services of Rockland in Nanuet (845-624-6325) and the Martin Luther King Multi Purpose Center in Spring Valley (845-425-8910). Call ahead to register and ask about lunch days.

faq.q: Do you have to pay for lunch at a New York senior center?
faq.a: No. NYSOFA says there is no charge for congregate meals. You are offered a chance to make a suggested voluntary contribution, such as $3.50 in Erie County or $3 in St. Lawrence County. Contributions are confidential and no one can be denied a meal for not giving.

faq.q: Can my spouse come to a senior center if they are under 60?
faq.a: Yes, for meals. NYSOFA says a spouse can get meals at a community dining site even if they are under 60. A person with a disability under 60 who lives with an older adult may use the site too. Some counties, such as St. Lawrence, charge a guest fee to other people under 60.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation to eat at a senior meal site?
faq.a: Often, yes. Erie County requires advance reservations, Westchester County requires pre-registration, and St. Lawrence County asks for 24 hours' notice. Call the site or your county Office for the Aging before the first visit.

faq.q: What if my parent can't get to a senior center?
faq.a: Ask about rides, since some sites provide transportation. If your parent can't prepare meals, they may qualify for home-delivered meals after an interview with the county Office for the Aging or NYC Aging. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to start.
